profile.name: Hula kahiko
profile.tagline: The traditional, unadorned dance of Hawaii performed to sacred chant and percussion.
profile.insight: In sacred hula, even a minor performance error was believed to invalidate the ritual, potentially bringing bad luck or dire consequences to the dancer.
profile.profile: Hula kahiko is the traditional Hawaiian dance form composed prior to 1894, performed without modern Western instrumentation. It dramatizes the poetic text of the mele (chant) through complex hand gestures and a foundational library of footwork. Accompanied by the oli (vocal chant) and percussion such as the pahu drum and ipu gourd, it serves as a living record of Hawaiian genealogy, mythology, and history.
profile.profile_long:
Hula kahiko represents the indigenous dance traditions of the Hawaiian Islands as they existed before significant Western influence. Defined as compositions created before 1894, this form is inextricably linked to the mele, or poetic text, which the dancer portrays through visual movement. In the absence of a written language, these dances and their accompanying chants served as the primary method for preserving Hawaiian history, including creation stories, royal genealogies, and significant cultural events. The dance is categorized into two main positions: noho (sitting) and luna (standing), with performers often divided by experience into 'olapa (dancers) and ho'opa'a (senior performers who may also chant and play instruments).

The practice of hula kahiko is deeply rooted in Hawaiian spirituality, particularly under the protection of the goddess Laka. Historically, students learning sacred hula were ritually secluded in a hālau (school) to prevent errors that could lead to spiritual misfortune. This reverence remains visible in modern performances, which are characterized by an austere aesthetic and traditional costuming. While the arrival of American Protestant missionaries in 1820 led to the suppression of hula, a cultural resurgence beginning in the late 1960s—often called the Hawaiian Renaissance—revitalized the form. Today, major events like the Merrie Monarch Festival provide a platform for hālau to demonstrate the technical precision and spiritual depth of the 'ai kahiko (ancient style).

Technically, hula kahiko is a complex language of the body. Hand motions are not merely decorative but represent specific natural phenomena, such as the swaying of trees or ocean waves, as well as human emotions like yearning or grief. These gestures are supported by a rhythmic foundation of foot and hip movements, including the kāholo (side-to-side step) and 'uwehe (knee spread). The music is strictly percussive and vocal, utilizing instruments like the pahu (sharkskin drum) and ipu heke (double gourd drum). Unlike the melodic, Western-influenced hula 'auana, hula kahiko maintains the rhythmic intensity and vocal textures of traditional oli, ensuring that the mana (spiritual power) of the Hawaiian language is preserved through performance.

sections.origins_and_history: Developed by Native Hawaiians who settled the islands, hula kahiko served as a vessel for oral history. Following the 1896 ban on the Hawaiian language in schools and the spread of Christianity, many traditional chants were viewed as pagan and lost. However, a resurgence in the late 1960s revitalized the practice, supported by institutions like Pūnana Leo immersion schools and the Merrie Monarch Festival, which began in 1971.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers use hand motions to represent words in a chant, such as waves or trees. Basic footwork includes the kāholo, kaʻo, kāwelu, hela, ʻuwehe, and ʻami. It can be performed sitting (noho) or standing (luna). Beginners learn in a hālau under a kumu (teacher), often starting with an oli kāhea to request permission to enter the training space.
sections.music_and_instruments: Performance is accompanied by oli (chant) and traditional percussion. Key instruments include the ipu (single gourd), ipu heke (double gourd), pahu (sharkskin drum), puniu (coconut knee drum), ʻiliʻili (lava stone castanets), ʻulīʻulī (feathered gourd rattles), pūʻili (split bamboo), and kālaʻau (rhythm sticks).
sections.costume_and_setting: Traditional female dancers wore a pāʻū (wrapped tapa skirt) and were originally topless, sometimes adding a layer of green kī leaves. Men wore the malo (loincloth). Both genders wear lei on the head (lei poʻo), neck, and wrists/ankles (kupeʻe). Materials are gathered from the forest after prayers to Laka; for sacred hula, these items are left as offerings on an altar after the dance.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Dances range from frivolous entertainment to solemn religious rites. Hula was performed to honor chiefs (aliʻi) as a form of fealty or to celebrate their lineage and name. Sacred hula performed at the heiau (temple) required absolute perfection to avoid bad luck.
sections.notable_figures: The goddess Laka is the patron of the hula and the forest. The kumu hula is the 'source of knowledge' or master teacher. King Kalākaua is noted for the 1883 coronation revival. Modern practitioners include those participating in the Merrie Monarch Festival.
sections.regional_variants: While related to Polynesian dances like the Tahitian 'ote'a or Maori haka, hula is unique to Hawaii. Sub-genres include hula pahu and hula ʻālaʻapapa (ancient), and 'ai kahiko (modern compositions in the ancient style).
sections.lineage: The tradition is passed down through hālau hula (schools). A hierarchy often exists from kumu (teacher) to alaka'i (leader), kokua (assistants), and 'olapa (dancers) or haumana (students).

profile.sacred_note: Sacred hula requires ritual seclusion during learning and absolute precision in performance; errors are seen as spiritually dangerous. Lei used in sacred dance are often left as offerings on an altar to Laka.

basic_steps: Hela (Pointing foot forward at an angle)
ʻUwehe (Lifting heels and pushing knees forward)
teaching.rhythm: Non-metered or rhythmic percussion based on the oli (chant)
teaching.formation: Standing (luna) or sitting (noho); often in rows facing the audience or chief
teaching.level_notes: Beginners are called haumana and must learn the protocol of the hālau, including the oli kāhea (entrance chant).

gaps: Specific choreography for 'ai kahiko (modern-ancient style) is not detailed.
Detailed rhythmic notation for specific percussion instruments is limited.

claims.text: Hula kahiko is defined as hula composed before 1894 without modern instruments.
claims.quote: Hula kahiko, often defined as those hula composed prior to 1894 which do not include modern instrumentation

claims.text: Performance errors in sacred hula were believed to have dire consequences.
claims.quote: even a minor error was considered to invalidate the performance. It might even be a presage of bad luck or have dire consequences.

claims.text: Dancers were ritually secluded under the protection of the goddess Laka during training.
claims.quote: they were ritually secluded and put under the protection of the goddess Laka during the learning period.

claims.text: The pahu drum is made of sharkskin and is considered a sacred instrument.
The Hawaiian language contains 43 different words to describe voice quality for chanting.
claims.quote: Hawaiian language contains 43 different words to describe voice quality; the technique and particularity of chanting styles is crucial
